To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(Ga,Mn)-doped InGaN MQWs are promising for optical spintronic applications, but that efficient spin injection requires further optimization of the device structure.

we have studied spin light-emitting devices with (Ga,Mn)/(In,Ga)N MQWs as active regions, and that we have found no spin polarization in these devices, due to the low efficiency of spin injection and spin relaxation.

the (Ga,MN)/InGaN multilayer diodes show a low conductivity of the (Ga,M)N layer, no or very low spin polarization in both (Ga,MN)N/InGaAs and (Ga,MN)/(In,Ga)N control samples, and a low efficiency of spin injection in the spin LED, due to spin relaxation losses during the energy dissipation process.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the optical and electrical characterization of the (Ga,MN)/InGaN multilayer structures grown by MBE, with the aim of studying the spin properties of the structures.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the (Ga,MN)N/InN MQW spin LED is not efficient for the spin injection and optical spin orientation.
spin losses in the spin LED are not related to the spin relaxation of the injected carriers, but to spin-dependent losses of the carriers during the relaxation to the exciton ground state.

the spin injection efficiency is very low in the studied (Ga,MnN/InGn)N structures, but that this does not exclude the possibility of efficient spin injection in other types of structures, e.g., with a different band alignment at the (Ga,MN)N/In(GaN) interface.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have demonstrated a spin LED with (Ga,Mn)-based spin injection and InGaN-based spin light emission, but we have failed to demonstrate a spin LED with efficient spin injection.

the optical spin orientation of excitons in InGaN MQWs and the electrical spin injection into (Ga,Mn)(N/InGn)/GaN heterostructures are not efficient processes in the studied structures, due to spin losses during energy relaxation.
the spin polarization in the (Ga,MN)/InGaN diode is very low, due to the low optical polarization in the InGaN QWs and the high spin losses during energy relaxation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the spin injection efficiency of (Ga,MN)N-based spin LEDs can be significantly increased by improving the electrical conductivity of (Ga,M)N and by reducing the parasitic current in the diodes.
the spin injection efficiency of (Ga,MN)N-based spin LEDs may be significantly lower than previously assumed.
the spin polarization in a spin light-emitting structure cannot be measured using the standard LED characterization methods.
